content:
# Deuteronomy 12 — Disagreement Log
**Chapter:** Deuteronomy 12 (32 verses) | **Arbiter:** SOPHIA

---

## V.1 — "statutes and ordinances" vs. "statutes and rules"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "the statutes and the ordinances which you shall be careful to do" |
| **LOGOS** | "the statutes and rules that you shall be careful to do" |
| **PNEUMA** | "the statutes and ordinances you must be careful to follow" |
| **SOPHIA** | "the statutes and the ordinances that you shall be careful to do" |

**Ruling:** "statutes and ordinances" — Hebrew chuqqim u-mishpatim. "Ordinances" (legal judgments) is the established project rendering for mishpatim. LOGOS's "rules" flattens the legal precision of the term. PNEUMA's "follow" for "do" (la'asot) also noted — consensus retains "do."

---

## V.1 — "upon the ground" vs. "on the earth" vs. "on earth"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "all the days that you live upon the ground" |
| **LOGOS** | "all the days that you live on the earth" |
| **PNEUMA** | "for as long as you live on earth" |
| **SOPHIA** | "all the days that you live on the earth" |

**Ruling:** "on the earth" — LOGOS. Hebrew ha-adamah = the ground/earth. EMET's "upon the ground" is more literal but slightly awkward; PNEUMA's restructuring ("for as long as") departs from the Hebrew clause order.

---

## V.2 — "surely destroy" vs. "completely demolish"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "You shall surely destroy all the places" |
| **LOGOS** | "You shall surely destroy all the places" |
| **PNEUMA** | "Completely demolish every place" |
| **SOPHIA** | "You shall utterly destroy all the places" |

**Ruling:** "utterly destroy" — Hebrew abed te'abedun is an absolute infinitive construction demanding intensification. EMET and LOGOS both use "surely" which is valid but "utterly" better captures the absolute force of the doubled verb form in the English Bible tradition. PNEUMA's "completely demolish" is accurate but "demolish" is too architectural for the Hebrew abed (to cause to perish/destroy).

---

## V.2 — "luxuriant tree" vs. "green tree" vs. "spreading tree"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "under every luxuriant tree" |
| **LOGOS** | "under every green tree" |
| **PNEUMA** | "under every spreading tree" |
| **SOPHIA** | "under every leafy tree" |

**Ruling:** "leafy tree" — Hebrew ra'anan = fresh/green/flourishing. EMET's "luxuriant" is accurate but slightly exotic; LOGOS's "green" is bland; PNEUMA's "spreading" imports a shape-description not in the Hebrew. "Leafy" (confirmed by LXX δασύ = thick/leafy) captures the dense-canopy shade of a cultic tree without over-interpreting.

---

## V.3 — "smash" vs. "dash in pieces"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "smash their pillars [masseboth]" |
| **LOGOS** | "dash in pieces their pillars" |
| **PNEUMA** | "smash their sacred pillars" |
| **SOPHIA** | "smash their pillars" |

**Ruling:** "smash their pillars" — EMET/PNEUMA. Hebrew shibbar = to shatter/smash. LOGOS's "dash in pieces" is archaic. PNEUMA adds "sacred" (not in Hebrew) — removed. EMET's bracketed [masseboth] retained in textual notes, not in the translation text.

---

## V.3 — "hew down" vs. "chop down" vs. "hack down"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "the carved images of their gods you shall hew down" |
| **LOGOS** | "You shall chop down the carved images of their gods" |
| **PNEUMA** | "hack down the carved images of their gods" |
| **SOPHIA** | "the carved images of their gods you shall cut down" |

**Ruling:** "cut down" — Hebrew gidda' = to cut/hew down. "Cut down" is the most neutral and widely understood English equivalent. EMET's "hew" is literary but faintly archaic; LOGOS's "chop" implies an axe-action correctly but is slightly colloquial; PNEUMA's "hack" implies violence more than precision.

---

## V.4 — "You shall not do so" vs. "You shall not worship...in that way"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "You shall not do so to the LORD your God." |
| **LOGOS** | "You shall not worship the LORD your God in that way." |
| **PNEUMA** | "You must not worship the LORD your God in the way they worshipped theirs." |
| **SOPHIA** | "You shall not do so to the LORD your God." |

**Ruling:** "You shall not do so to the LORD your God" — EMET. Hebrew lo-ta'asun ken = "you shall not do so." The verse is deliberately terse and covers a range of possible prohibited actions — not only worship patterns but the destruction of YHWH's altar. LOGOS and PNEUMA both insert "worship" as an interpretive narrowing. The bare "do so" preserves the verse's pointed ambiguity.

---

## V.5 — "his dwelling" vs. "make his habitation there" vs. "as his dwelling"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "to put his name — his dwelling [shekhinato] — there" |
| **LOGOS** | "to put his name and make his habitation there" |
| **PNEUMA** | "to put his name there as his dwelling" |
| **SOPHIA** | "to put his name — to make his dwelling there" |

**Ruling:** "to make his dwelling there" — the Ketiv/Qere variation at this verse (leshikhno vs. leshakken shemo) is acknowledged. The consensus rendering preserves "dwelling" (EMET/PNEUMA) while avoiding EMET's bracketed Hebrew gloss in the text. LOGOS's "habitation" is slightly archaic.

---

## V.6 — "contribution of your hand" vs. "contribution that you present" vs. "your contributions"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "the contribution of your hand" |
| **LOGOS** | "the contribution that you present" |
| **PNEUMA** | "your contributions" |
| **SOPHIA** | "the contribution of your hand" |

**Ruling:** "the contribution of your hand" — EMET. Hebrew terumah yedkhem = the contribution/offering of your hands. The hand-gesture language is significant; terumah is a hand-raised offering. LOGOS dissolves the image; PNEUMA loses it entirely.

---

## V.7 — "putting-forth of your hand" vs. "all that you undertake" vs. "everything your hands have worked for"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "in all the putting-forth of your hand" |
| **LOGOS** | "in all that you undertake" |
| **PNEUMA** | "because of everything your hands have worked for" |
| **SOPHIA** | "in all that you put your hand to" |

**Ruling:** "all that you put your hand to" — a natural English idiom rendering mishloach yadkhem (the sending-forth of your hand). EMET is accurate but wooden; LOGOS abandons the hand-imagery; PNEUMA's "worked for" introduces a labor-accomplishment idea not in the Hebrew.

---

## V.8 — "every man" vs. "everyone" (gender-specific vs. inclusive)

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "every man [doing] what is right in his own eyes" |
| **LOGOS** | "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" |
| **PNEUMA** | "everyone doing whatever seems right in their own eyes" |
| **SOPHIA** | "each man doing what is right in his own eyes" |

**Ruling:** "each man doing what is right in his own eyes" — Hebrew ish = man (masculine singular). The masculine singular is retained because it is theologically specific — ish is the individual male head of household, not a generic collective. The phrase echoes Judges 17:6 and 21:25 where ish is similarly used. PNEUMA's plural "their own eyes" smooths over the Hebrew and loses the Judges resonance.

---

## V.10 — "Yarden" vs. "Jordan"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "you shall cross over the Yarden" |
| **LOGOS** | "when you go over the Jordan" |
| **PNEUMA** | "when you cross the Jordan" |
| **SOPHIA** | "when you cross over the Jordan" |

**Ruling:** "the Jordan" — established English name form. Project convention uses English name forms throughout (cf. DEU_011 ruling on "Dathan and Abiram"). EMET's "Yarden" is consistent with Hebrew transliteration practice but the project standard is English forms for proper names.

---

## V.10 — "dwell in security" vs. "live in safety"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "you shall dwell in security" |
| **LOGOS** | "so that you live in safety" |
| **PNEUMA** | "so that you are living in safety" |
| **SOPHIA** | "so that you dwell in safety" |

**Ruling:** "dwell in safety" — Hebrew yashab + betach. "Dwell" (yashab) is literal and appropriate. "Safety" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is preferred over EMET's "security" — betach implies unafraid, relaxed dwelling rather than fortified security.

---

## V.11 — "cause his name to dwell there" vs. "make his name dwell there" vs. "as a dwelling for his name"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "to cause his name to dwell there [leshakken shemo sham]" |
| **LOGOS** | "to make his name dwell there" |
| **PNEUMA** | "as a dwelling for his name" |
| **SOPHIA** | "to make his name dwell there" |

**Ruling:** "to make his name dwell there" — LOGOS. The leshakken shemo sham formula is the purest Deuteronomic Name theology expression. EMET's "cause his name to dwell" is technically accurate (shakan in Hiphil = cause to dwell) but heavier; LOGOS's "make...dwell" is equivalent and more natural. PNEUMA's "dwelling for his name" inverts the verbal force into a noun phrase.

---

## V.11 — "choice vow-offerings" vs. "finest vow offerings"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "your choice vow-offerings which you vow" |
| **LOGOS** | "all your finest vow offerings that you vow" |
| **PNEUMA** | "all the choice vow offerings you make" |
| **SOPHIA** | "all your choice vow offerings that you vow" |

**Ruling:** "choice vow offerings" — EMET/PNEUMA. Hebrew mivchar nidreikhem = your choice/select vow offerings. "Finest" (LOGOS) is synonymous but "choice" is slightly more precise as a translation of mivchar. "That you vow" preserved per Hebrew tidberu.

---

## V.12 — "within your gates" vs. "within your towns"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "the Levite who is within your gates" |
| **LOGOS** | "the Levite that is within your towns" |
| **PNEUMA** | "the Levites from your towns" |
| **SOPHIA** | "the Levite who is within your gates" |

**Ruling:** "within your gates" — EMET. Hebrew bish'arekhem = within your gates. Project convention preserves "gates" as the Deuteronomic idiom for community/settlement (cf. consistent ruling in DEU_010–011). LOGOS and PNEUMA modernize to "towns" — accurate but loses the Hebrew idiom. Also, "the Levite who is" (singular) vs. PNEUMA's "the Levites from" (plural) — Hebrew is singular (ha-Levi).

---

## V.13 — "Be careful lest" vs. "Take care that you do not"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "Be careful lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see." |
| **LOGOS** | "Take care that you do not offer your burnt offerings at any place that you see" |
| **PNEUMA** | "Be careful that you do not offer your burnt offerings anywhere you please" |
| **SOPHIA** | "Take care lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see." |

**Ruling:** "Take care lest you offer...in every place that you see" — combining LOGOS's "Take care" with EMET's "lest" and "in every place that you see." Hebrew hishamer-lekha pen + "bekhol maqom asher tir'eh" = in every place that you see. PNEUMA's "anywhere you please" paraphrases the Hebrew's visual-spatial grounding ("that you see").

---

## V.15 — "in all the desire of your soul" vs. "as much as you desire" vs. "wherever you wish"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "in all the desire of your soul you may slaughter and eat meat" |
| **LOGOS** | "you may slaughter and eat meat within any of your towns, as much as you desire" |
| **PNEUMA** | "you may slaughter and eat meat wherever you wish within any of your towns" |
| **SOPHIA** | "in all the craving of your soul you may slaughter and eat meat" |

**Ruling:** "in all the craving of your soul" — EMET's structure is preserved. Hebrew bekhol-avvat nafshekha = in all the craving/desire of your soul. "Craving" is sharper than "desire" for avvah (craving, appetite); nefesh (soul) is preserved as the subject of the craving. LOGOS relocates the clause; PNEUMA misidentifies the freedom as spatial ("wherever you wish") rather than quantitative/unlimited.

---

## V.17 — "new wine" vs. "wine" / "fresh oil" vs. "oil"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "the tithe of your grain and of your new wine and of your fresh oil" |
| **LOGOS** | "the tithe of your grain or of your wine or of your oil" |
| **PNEUMA** | "the tithe of your grain, wine, or olive oil" |
| **SOPHIA** | "the tithe of your grain and of your new wine and of your fresh oil" |

**Ruling:** "new wine" and "fresh oil" — EMET. Hebrew tirosh = new wine (unfermented grape juice / new vintage) and yitshar = fresh oil (pressed oil). These are distinct terms from yayin (aged wine) and shemen (oil generally). LOGOS and PNEUMA both flatten to generic "wine" and "oil," losing the specificity of the Hebrew vocabulary. The "and...and...and" conjunction (three separate items with ve-) is also preserved.

---

## V.18 — "all that you put your hand to" vs. "all that you undertake"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "in all the putting-forth of your hand" |
| **LOGOS** | "in all that you undertake" |
| **PNEUMA** | "in everything your hands work toward" |
| **SOPHIA** | "in all that you put your hand to" |

**Ruling:** "in all that you put your hand to" — consistent with ruling at v.7. The hand-imagery of mishloach yadkhem is maintained.

---

## V.19 — "forsake" vs. "neglect"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "lest you forsake the Levite all your days upon your ground" |
| **LOGOS** | "that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land" |
| **PNEUMA** | "not to neglect the Levite for as long as you live in your land" |
| **SOPHIA** | "lest you forsake the Levite all your days on your ground" |

**Ruling:** "forsake" — EMET. Hebrew azab = to abandon/forsake/leave behind. This is a strong word — the same root is used of leaving one's father and mother (Gen. 2:24). "Neglect" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is too mild. Also, "all your days upon your ground" (EMET) is more literal than "as long as you live in your land." "Ground" (ha-adamah) echoes v.1.

---

## V.20 — craving phrasing and structure

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "and you say, 'I will eat meat' — because your soul craves to eat meat — according to all the desire of your soul you may eat meat" |
| **LOGOS** | "and you say, 'I will eat meat,' because you crave meat, you may eat meat whenever you desire" |
| **PNEUMA** | "and you crave meat and say, 'I want to eat meat,' you may eat as much meat as you wish" |
| **SOPHIA** | "and you say, 'I will eat meat' — because your soul craves to eat meat — in all the craving of your soul you may eat meat" |

**Ruling:** EMET's structure with the parenthetical dash is preserved. Hebrew: ve'amarta oklah basar = "and you say, 'I will eat meat'"; ki-teavveh nafshekha = "because your soul craves"; bekhol-avvat nafshekha = "in all the craving of your soul." The nefesh-craving chain is a deliberate repetition. "Craving" (avvah) replaces "desire" for precision.

---

## V.21 — "as I commanded you" vs. "as I have commanded you"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "as I commanded you" |
| **LOGOS** | "as I have commanded you" |
| **PNEUMA** | "as I have commanded you" |
| **SOPHIA** | "as I commanded you" |

**Ruling:** "as I commanded you" — EMET. Hebrew ka'asher tsivvitikha = as I commanded you (simple past). The past tense is the Hebrew here. LOGOS/PNEUMA's perfect "have commanded" is slightly more English-idiomatic but the simple past is accurate.

---

## V.23 — "be strong not to eat" vs. "be sure that you do not eat" vs. "be very firm on this point"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "Only be strong not to eat the blood" |
| **LOGOS** | "Only be sure that you do not eat the blood" |
| **PNEUMA** | "But be very firm on this point: do not eat the blood" |
| **SOPHIA** | "Only be strong not to eat the blood" |

**Ruling:** "Only be strong not to eat the blood" — EMET. Hebrew raq chazaq = only be strong/resolute. Chazaq is the word used for strengthening oneself for battle or for difficult tasks (cf. Josh. 1:6–9). Applying it to a dietary restriction is rhetorically striking and should not be smoothed. LOGOS's "be sure" and PNEUMA's "be very firm" both soften the Hebrew idiom. EMET's rendering is the most faithful and most interesting.

---

## V.23 — "the blood — it is the life" vs. "the blood is the life"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "for the blood — it is the life [dam hu ha-nefesh]" |
| **LOGOS** | "for the blood is the life" |
| **PNEUMA** | "for the blood is the life" |
| **SOPHIA** | "for the blood — it is the life" |

**Ruling:** "for the blood — it is the life" — EMET. Hebrew ki ha-dam hu ha-nefesh = "for the blood, it [is] the life." The pronoun hu (it/he) creates a formal predicate equation: dam = ha-nefesh. The dash in the English reproduces this syntax. LOGOS and PNEUMA both produce smooth English sentences but lose the equation structure.

---

## V.23 — "meat" vs. "flesh" (ba-basar)

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "you shall not eat the life together with the meat" |
| **LOGOS** | "you shall not eat the life with the flesh" |
| **PNEUMA** | "you must not eat the life with the meat" |
| **SOPHIA** | "you shall not eat the life together with the meat" |

**Ruling:** "meat" — EMET/PNEUMA. Hebrew ba-basar = with the flesh/meat. In the secular slaughter context of vv.15–25, "meat" is the appropriate English register. "Flesh" (LOGOS) is more appropriate in sacrificial/ritual contexts (cf. ruling at v.27). "Together with" (EMET) preserves the prepositional marker of the Hebrew more precisely than bare "with."

---

## V.25 — "your sons after you" vs. "your children after you"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "with you and with your sons after you" |
| **LOGOS** | "with you and with your children after you" |
| **PNEUMA** | "for you and for your children after you" |
| **SOPHIA** | "with you and with your sons after you" |

**Ruling:** "your sons after you" — EMET. Hebrew u-vanekha acharekha = and your sons after you. Hebrew ben/banim (sons) is specific; "children" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is inclusive but generalizes the Hebrew. Project convention preserves gender-specific terms where the Hebrew is specific.

---

## V.27 — "the meat and the blood" vs. "the flesh and the blood"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "the meat and the blood, upon the altar" |
| **LOGOS** | "the flesh and the blood, on the altar" |
| **PNEUMA** | "the meat and the blood — on the altar" |
| **SOPHIA** | "the flesh and the blood — on the altar" |

**Ruling:** "the flesh and the blood" — LOGOS. Hebrew ha-basar veha-dam. In the sacrificial context of v.27 (altar offerings), "flesh" is the appropriate register — sacrificial texts throughout Leviticus and Numbers use "flesh" for basar in ritual settings. The distinction from "meat" in the secular passages (vv.15, 23) is intentional.

---

## V.27 — "poured out against the altar" vs. "poured out on the altar" vs. "poured out beside the altar"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out against the altar" |
| **LOGOS** | "The blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out on the altar" |
| **PNEUMA** | "The blood of your sacrifices must be poured out beside the altar" |
| **SOPHIA** | "the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out on the altar" |

**Ruling:** "poured out on the altar" — LOGOS. Hebrew yishafekh al-hamizbeach = shall be poured out upon/on the altar. EMET's "against" is overly literal (al can mean "upon" or "against" but the ritual context is clearly pouring onto the altar base); PNEUMA's "beside" is too distant. "On the altar" is correct.

---

## V.28 — "Keep and hear" vs. "Be careful to obey" vs. "Be careful to obey"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "Keep and hear all these words which I am commanding you" |
| **LOGOS** | "Be careful to obey all these words that I command you" |
| **PNEUMA** | "Be careful to obey all these words I am commanding you" |
| **SOPHIA** | "Keep and hear all these words that I am commanding you" |

**Ruling:** "Keep and hear" — EMET. Hebrew shemor veshama'ta = keep and hear/heed. These are two distinct verbs: shaman (to keep/guard/observe) and shama' (to hear/heed). LOGOS and PNEUMA both collapse both verbs into a single "Be careful to obey," which loses the two-verb Deuteronomic pairing. The pair "keep and hear" is a characteristic Deuteronomic structure (cf. Deut. 5:1, 6:3).

---

## V.29 — sentence structure and "before you"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "When the LORD your God cuts off the nations to whom you are going in to dispossess them from before you" |
| **LOGOS** | "When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations whom you go in to dispossess" |
| **PNEUMA** | "When the LORD your God has cut off before you the nations that you are going in to drive out" |
| **SOPHIA** | "When the LORD your God cuts off before you the nations to whom you are going in to dispossess them" |

**Ruling:** "cuts off before you the nations to whom you are going in to dispossess them" — combining LOGOS's placement of "before you" with EMET's "to whom you are going in to dispossess them." Hebrew yakrith...mipanekha = cuts off...from before you. The "from before you" is directional language; LOGOS places "before you" naturally. EMET's "from before you" at the end is literal but awkward.

---

## V.30 — "be ensnared after them" vs. "ensnared to follow them" vs. "ensnared into imitating them"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "lest you be ensnared after them after their being destroyed from before you" |
| **LOGOS** | "that you be not ensnared to follow them, after they have been destroyed before you" |
| **PNEUMA** | "that you are not ensnared into imitating them after they have been destroyed before you" |
| **SOPHIA** | "lest you be ensnared following after them after they are destroyed from before you" |

**Ruling:** "lest you be ensnared following after them" — Hebrew tinaqqesh achareihem = you be snared after them. "After them" (achareihem) is theologically loaded — it is the language of discipleship and devotion: to go "after" a deity is to become its follower. PNEUMA's "imitating" is too cognitive; it misses the devotional-directional force of achareihem. "Following after them" is a slight paraphrase but captures the movement. LOGOS drops "after them" entirely.

---

## V.31 — "abomination [to'evah]" vs. "abominable thing" vs. "detestable to the LORD — things he hates"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "every abomination [to'evah] which the LORD hates they did for their gods" |
| **LOGOS** | "every abominable thing that the LORD hates they have done for their gods" |
| **PNEUMA** | "everything they do for their gods is detestable to the LORD — things he hates" |
| **SOPHIA** | "every abomination that the LORD hates they did for their gods" |

**Ruling:** "every abomination that the LORD hates they did for their gods" — EMET without the bracketed gloss. "Abomination" is the established English rendering of to'evah (cf. DEU_011 pattern and Leviticus rulings). LOGOS's "abominable thing" is slightly weaker. PNEUMA restructures the sentence and doubles the condemnation ("detestable...things he hates") — the Hebrew has one relative clause, not two.

---

## V.32 — "Every word" vs. "Everything"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "Every word which I am commanding you — it you shall keep to do" |
| **LOGOS** | "Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do." |
| **PNEUMA** | "Everything I am commanding you, be careful to do it." |
| **SOPHIA** | "Every word that I am commanding you — it you shall be careful to do" |

**Ruling:** "Every word that I am commanding you" — EMET. Hebrew kol-hadavar = every word/the whole word. Davar is "word" (not merely "thing") — the covenant is a verbal, spoken, textual deposit. The canonical closing formula "do not add...do not diminish" applies to the davar — the word. Translating as "everything" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) loses the word-as-covenant sense. The emphatic pronoun + verb ("it you shall be careful to do") is also preserved from EMET.

---

## V.32 — "add upon it" vs. "add to it" / "diminish from it" vs. "take from it" vs. "subtract from it"

| | Translation |
|---|---|
| **EMET** | "you shall not add upon it and you shall not diminish from it" |
| **LOGOS** | "You shall not add to it or take from it." |
| **PNEUMA** | "Do not add to it or subtract from it." |
| **SOPHIA** | "you shall not add to it and you shall not diminish from it" |

**Ruling:** "you shall not add to it and you shall not diminish from it" — EMET. Hebrew lo tosef alav = you shall not add to/upon it; velo tigra' mimmennu = and you shall not diminish/take away from it. The two negative jussives are connected by ve- (and) not "or" (LOGOS/PNEUMA). "And" preserves both as independent absolute prohibitions. "Diminish" (EMET) is more precise than LOGOS's "take from" or PNEUMA's "subtract" for the Hebrew gara' (to diminish, to curtail).

---

**Total disagreements logged: 37**

— SOPHIA
